newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU bankers support idea of fixing EMU rates early.
newsitem.headline: EU bankers support idea of fixing EMU rates early.

text.p: The European Banking Federation said on Tuesday it supported a plan by the European Monetary Institute to pre-announce a method for fixing the conversion rates of currencies joining a single currency in 1999.

The proposal, advanced by Alexandre Lamfalussy, the EMI's president, would produce a formula in early 1998 for calculating the exchange rates among the countries entering economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We think it is more secure to have an average of all the rates over six months," Karl-Heinz Wessel, president of the Federation told a news conference.
"Brussels should announce it early in 1998 together with the countries chosen," he added.

At issue is the risky period between early 1998, when the EU will decide which countries qualify for the monetary union, and 1999, when participating national currencies would become fixed amongst themselves and to the single currency.
Nearly all are against accepting the rates which exist in the market on January 1, 1999, for fear that it could leave the currencies involved exposed to destabilising market speculation.

The Federation, representing a broad cross-section of banks in the 15-nation bloc, also said it supported access for non-EMU central banks to TARGET (Trans-European Automated Real-Time Gross Settlement Express Transfer system).

TARGET is a currency clearing system due to start in 1999 among banks in the single currency bloc. There are questions, however, over whether full access to the system should be allowed for central banks outside the bloc.

Britain, in particular, has argued that such discrimination would be illegal under the EU's single market legislation. But others say banks outside a common currency should not have the same privileges as those within.
Nickolaus Bomcke, secretary general of the Federation, said the group's position on non-discrimination did not necessarily mean full access.
"Obviously countries outside may have to be distinguished, but it should not be an unfair distinction," Bomcke told the news conference.
The Federation would also like a future European Central Bank to avoid the use of minimum reserves in implementing monetary policy.
For competitive reasons, the group saw disadvantages to banks within the EMU zone who needed to put aside a certain percentage of their reserves.
They said such a plan would likely increase costs and lead to higher borrowing rates for consumers and businesses.
